title: Oil and the Gulf: two straits, one cartel and a war premium
hook:
Look at a map of the Gulf and find the point where Iran's coast almost touches the tip of Oman. That gap, the Strait of Hormuz, is one of the most important stretches of water on Earth. Tankers carrying a large share of the world's oil squeeze through it in narrow shipping lanes, day and night. For India, which imports most of the crude it burns, it is something close to a jugular vein.

Indian oil planners have spent decades gaming out what happens if Hormuz shuts. In 2026 they stopped gaming. After US and Israeli strikes on Iran began in late February, Iran closed the strait. A ceasefire from April collapsed by July. Brent crude has risen by about half over the course of the war, and tankers are still being attacked despite emergency releases from oil stockpiles.

So how exactly does a war in the Gulf reach an Indian paint company, an airline, a state-run refiner and the rupee? Why do some oil spikes fade in weeks while others last for months? And who, if anyone, in the Indian market comes out ahead? That is what this chapter untangles.
short: Most of India's crude passes through two narrow stretches of water: the Strait of Hormuz for Gulf oil and the Bab-el-Mandeb at the mouth of the Red Sea for cargoes from the west. Geopolitics enters India's economy mostly through those two points.
A demand-led oil rise comes with global growth and Indian cyclicals can ride it. A supply-led rise, from war, sanctions or a blocked route, is a pure tax on India.
Oil reaches Indian stocks through the rupee, inflation, the government's budget and company margins, in roughly that order of speed.
The war premium in a supply shock fades when the route reopens, often abruptly. That is why oil round-tripped within weeks after Abqaiq in 2019 but stayed high for months in 2022.

OPEC+ spare capacity is the slow variable underneath: it decides how much of a disruption can be offset. When the disruption is Hormuz itself, much of that spare capacity is stuck behind the same strait.

sections.heading: Two narrow stretches of water decide India's oil bill
sections.html:
India imports the large majority of the crude it uses, and the single biggest source is the Gulf: Iraq, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait. Almost all of that has to leave the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz. So does much of India's cooking gas and the liquefied natural gas it buys from Qatar. By most estimates, roughly half of India's crude imports pass through that one strait.

The second chokepoint is the Bab-el-Mandeb, the narrow mouth of the Red Sea between Yemen and the Horn of Africa. Cargoes coming from the west, Russian crude from the Baltic and Black Sea, oil from the Mediterranean, pass through the Suez Canal and down the Red Sea to reach India. If that route is unsafe, ships go the long way round Africa, past the Cape of Good Hope.

[[fig:1]]

The schematic shows India's main crude routes, not to scale. The two red points are the chokepoints that matter most. Notice that the Gulf route is short and direct, which is why Gulf oil is cheap to bring home. The Cape route, by contrast, adds weeks to a voyage and a big jump in freight cost. And notice where the alternative suppliers sit: the US and West Africa are on the long Atlantic routes, so replacing Gulf oil in a hurry means paying more for both the oil and the shipping.

There are partial escape hatches. Saudi Arabia has a pipeline that carries crude across the desert to its Red Sea coast, and the UAE has one that reaches a port outside the strait. But they can carry only a fraction of what normally flows through Hormuz. When the strait closes, there is no full substitute.

sections.heading: Not every oil spike is the same animal
sections.html:
Before reacting to any rise in oil, ask the most important question in this chapter: why is it rising?

A demand-led rise happens when the world economy is booming. Factories run hot, people fly and drive more, and oil gets dearer because everyone wants more of it. That hurts India's import bill, but it comes with strong global demand for Indian goods, services and metals. Indian cyclicals can rise alongside oil. The supercycle of the mid-2000s, which peaked in 2008, was largely this kind.

A supply-led rise is a different beast. A war, a sanction or a blocked shipping lane removes barrels from the market while demand stays the same. Oil gets dearer not because the world is richer but because it is scarcer. For an importer like India there is no offsetting boom. It is simply a transfer of money from Indian consumers and companies to oil producers: a pure tax.

A demand-led oil rise comes with a party. A supply-led one comes with the bill and no party.

The two kinds also end differently. Demand-led peaks end when demand cracks, as in the 2008 crisis, when oil collapsed along with the world economy. Supply-led spikes end when the supply comes back: the sanction is lifted, the plant is repaired, the route reopens. That ending can be sudden, which matters enormously for timing, as we will see.

Today's rise is clearly supply-led. Nobody is buying more oil because the world is booming. Barrels are trapped behind a closed strait.

sections.heading: Follow a barrel through India's economy
sections.html:
So how does dear oil actually travel through India? Follow the money, roughly in order of speed.

  • The rupee, within days. Refiners need more dollars to pay for the same crude. That extra demand for dollars widens India's current account deficit, the gap between what the country earns from the world and what it pays. A wider gap needs foreign money to fill it, and if that money is nervous, the rupee falls. A weaker rupee then makes the oil dearer still in rupee terms.
  • Inflation, within weeks to months. Some of the hit is direct: petrol, diesel, cooking gas, airfares. Much more is indirect. Diesel moves almost everything in India, from vegetables to cement, so a costlier diesel raises prices across the economy a few months later. That is what pushes the RBI to tighten.
  • The budget, over months. Pump prices in India are officially market-linked, but governments hate raising them, especially near elections. So the state cuts excise duty on fuel, raises subsidies on cooking gas and pays more for fertiliser made from imported gas. Every rupee of relief is a rupee of extra borrowing or spending cut elsewhere.
  • Company margins, over quarters. State-run fuel retailers can be asked to hold pump prices and absorb the losses. Paint, tyre, chemical and plastics makers face dearer raw materials. Airlines face their biggest cost rising. Most of them recover the cost eventually, but with a lag of a quarter or two.

Here's the thing that makes oil uniquely nasty for India: it hits all four at once, and each makes the others worse. A weaker rupee raises inflation, higher inflation forces tighter money, tighter money slows growth, and slower growth shrinks the tax revenue the government needs for fuel relief. It is a single shock that wears four different masks.

sections.heading: The war premium: priced in by panic, priced out by a reopened route
sections.html:
When a supply shock hits, the oil price contains two parts. One is the normal price set by supply and demand. The other is a war premium: the extra traders pay because they fear the disruption will spread or last. The premium is a bet on the future, and like any bet it can unwind in an afternoon.

That is why the duration of a supply shock depends almost entirely on how long the physical disruption lasts. When drones hit Saudi Arabia's giant Abqaiq processing plant in 2019, the price spiked violently and then gave it all back within weeks, because Saudi Aramco repaired the damage far faster than feared. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the disruption came from sanctions that stayed in place, so the high prices lasted months.

[[fig:2]]

The chart shows Brent since mid-2015. Look at the shape of each spike. Abqaiq is barely a blip. The 2022 spike is a tall mountain that took most of the year to come down. The Covid collapse in 2020 is the opposite case: a demand shock that briefly sent prices to their lowest in decades. And the last stretch, the Iran war, shows the price climbing back towards the 2022 highs, with violent swings as ceasefire hopes rose and collapsed.

For investors this creates a specific trap. By the time a supply shock is front-page news, the war premium is fully priced. The big move often comes when the route reopens, and it comes fast, sometimes before the news has fully sunk in. That is why the single most important signpost for Indian equities in a Gulf crisis is not the oil price itself but the status of the route.

sections.heading: OPEC+: the slow hand on the tap
sections.html:
Underneath the wars and drone strikes sits a slower force: the oil producers' cartel. OPEC, led by Saudi Arabia, has tried to manage the oil price for decades. Since late 2016 it has worked with Russia and a handful of other producers under the name OPEC+, coordinating how much oil each member pumps.

The key number to understand is spare capacity: oil that producers could pump quickly but choose not to. It acts like a shock absorber. If a war takes barrels off the market, members with spare capacity can open the taps and cushion the blow. If spare capacity is thin, every disruption goes straight into the price.

OPEC+ policy is a constant tug of war between what producers want and what importers can bear. Saudi Arabia needs oil prices high enough to fund its budget and its huge development plans. Russia needs revenue. India, as one of the world's largest importers, wants prices low and has never been shy about saying so, which has occasionally led to sharp public exchanges, as you will see in the history below.

But here is the cruel twist in a Hormuz crisis. Most of the world's spare capacity sits in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait, the very countries whose oil has to pass through the strait. If the strait is closed, the shock absorber is stuck on the wrong side of the problem. That is why a Hormuz closure is categorically worse than a loss of the same number of barrels anywhere else, and why emergency releases from government stockpiles become the main line of defence.

sections.heading: Freight and insurance: where chokepoint risk shows up first
sections.html:
Crude prices get the headlines, but chokepoint risk usually shows up first somewhere less glamorous: the cost of shipping and insuring a tanker.

When a route becomes dangerous, three things happen. Insurers add war-risk premiums for every voyage through the area. Shipowners demand higher charter rates to send their vessels and crews into harm's way, or refuse altogether. And ships that re-route take longer, which effectively shrinks the number of tankers available and pushes rates up everywhere.

The Red Sea crisis of 2023 and 2024 showed this clearly. Attacks on shipping by Yemen's Houthi rebels pushed most big container lines and many tankers to sail around Africa. Crude prices barely moved for much of that period, because no oil was actually lost. But freight costs jumped, delivery times stretched, and Indian exporters shipping goods to Europe found their margins squeezed by shipping bills.

So when you watch a Gulf crisis, watch freight and insurance alongside Brent. If freight is rising and crude is not, the market is pricing route risk rather than lost supply. If both are rising, as now, the market believes barrels are genuinely missing.

sections.heading: Winners and losers inside the Indian market
sections.html:
A supply-led oil shock is mostly a tax on India, but it does not tax everyone equally.

The clearest losers are businesses that burn oil or use it as a raw material and cannot raise prices quickly: airlines, paint makers, tyre companies, chemical and plastics firms, and logistics companies. State-run fuel retailers can be the biggest losers of all if the government asks them to hold pump prices, as it did for long stretches in 2022.

The apparent winners are upstream producers, the companies that pump crude in India and sell it at world prices. Their earnings should jump. But history teaches caution: in 2022 the government imposed a windfall tax on domestic crude producers and on fuel exports, clawing back much of the gain. In India, an oil windfall is a political event, not just a financial one.

Then there are the Gulf links that people forget. Millions of Indians work in the Gulf and send money home; Kerala in particular depends on it. A war that disrupts Gulf economies can hit those remittances, and with them a steady source of dollars for India. Indian exporters who sell food, textiles and engineering goods to Gulf markets face disrupted orders and shipping.

Finally, every listed company feels the indirect hit through the rupee and interest rates. That is why even businesses with no direct oil exposure tend to fall in a Gulf crisis, and why they tend to bounce hardest when it ends.

history.title: The embargo and the revolution
history.story:
In October 1973, during the war between Israel and its Arab neighbours, Arab oil producers led by Saudi Arabia's King Faisal cut output and embargoed oil to the United States and others. Saudi oil minister Sheikh Ahmed Zaki Yamani became the most famous face in the world of oil. Within months the price of crude had quadrupled. Americans queued for hours at petrol stations, and India, already short of foreign exchange, saw its import bill soar and inflation surge.

India's response was to look for its own oil. In February 1974 the drilling rig Sagar Samrat struck oil off the coast of Bombay, the discovery that became Bombay High. Then, in 1979, the Iranian revolution toppled the Shah and triggered a second oil shock, and the world slid into stagflation.
history.lesson: Supply shocks reprice oil in weeks and can last years, and two in quick succession are the classic recipe for stagflation.

history.title: The biggest airlift in history
history.story:
In August 1990 Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded Kuwait. Within a couple of months oil prices had doubled. For India the blow came twice: a far larger oil bill, and the sudden loss of money sent home by Indian workers in Kuwait and Iraq.

Well over a hundred thousand Indians were stranded. Over roughly two months, Indians were bussed across the desert to Amman in Jordan, and Air India flew them home in hundreds of flights, an operation recognised as the largest evacuation by a civilian airline ever. But the economic damage was done. The Gulf war pushed India's already fragile finances over the edge, and by the summer of 1991 the country was pledging its gold to avoid a default.
history.lesson: A Gulf war hits India twice, through oil and through remittances, and that double blow is what turned a bad year into the crisis of 1991.

history.title: The drones that hit Abqaiq
history.story:
Early one Saturday in September 2019, drones and missiles struck Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq processing plant and the Khurais oilfield, briefly knocking out about half of Saudi Arabia's output. Yemen's Houthis claimed the attack; Washington blamed Iran. When markets opened on Monday, oil posted one of its biggest one-day jumps in decades.

Then Aramco did something nobody expected: it restored production within weeks. The war premium evaporated. The Nifty dipped on the day and slid a little further over the next fortnight, but within six weeks it was well higher. Part of that was luck: the same week, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced a surprise cut in corporate tax, and the Sensex had its biggest one-day gain in over a decade.
history.lesson: Supply shocks that are quickly repaired fade within weeks; selling into the first spike is usually the expensive mistake.

history.title: The price war, and the advice India didn't want
history.story:
OPEC+ was born in late 2016, when Saudi Arabia and Russia agreed to coordinate output. In March 2020, as Covid spread, the alliance blew apart at a meeting in Vienna: Russia's Alexander Novak refused deeper cuts, and Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman responded by flooding the market. Demand collapsed at the same time, and in April US crude futures briefly traded below zero. India quietly filled its underground strategic reserves at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur with dirt-cheap oil.

A year later, OPEC+ was holding back supply and prices had recovered. When India's oil minister Dharmendra Pradhan pressed for relief, Prince Abdulaziz suggested India draw on the cheap oil it had bought the year before. Pradhan called the advice undiplomatic, and state refiners promptly cut their Saudi purchases.
history.lesson: OPEC+ manages prices for producers, not importers, so India's best defence is diversified suppliers and the nerve to buy when oil is cheap.

history.title: Russia's discount barrels
history.story:
When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Brent shot to its highest level since 2008 and the Nifty fell sharply on the day. As Western buyers shunned Russian crude, Indian refiners did the opposite, buying discounted Russian barrels in huge volumes. Within a year Russia had gone from a minor supplier to India's largest.

At home, the government kept pump prices frozen for months, and the state fuel retailers took heavy losses. In July it slapped a windfall tax on domestic crude producers and on fuel exports, a tax that stayed in place until late 2024. Sanctions kept the shock alive far longer than Abqaiq.
history.lesson: Sanctions-driven shocks last as long as the sanctions, and in India the government decides who absorbs the cost.

history.title: The Red Sea goes dark
history.story:
After the Gaza war began in late 2023, Yemen's Houthi rebels started attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea, hijacking a car carrier and firing drones and missiles at tankers. The world's big shipping lines diverted around Africa. In December 2023 a drone hit the tanker Chem Pluto, carrying Indian crew, off the coast of Gujarat; the Pentagon blamed Iran. The Indian Navy sent guided-missile destroyers to patrol the Arabian Sea.

Crude prices stayed surprisingly calm, because no oil was actually lost. But freight rates jumped and voyages to Europe stretched by weeks.
history.lesson: Chokepoint risk shows up in freight before it shows up in crude.

history.title: Hormuz closes
history.story:
In late February 2026 the United States and Israel began strikes on Iran. Iran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz, the scenario India's oil-security planners had feared for decades. A ceasefire from April raised hopes, but it collapsed by July and attacks on Gulf shipping resumed despite emergency releases of oil from government stockpiles.

Over the course of the war Brent has risen by about half. For India it has meant scrambling for cargoes from further afield, a weaker rupee, rising inflation and pressure on the RBI to tighten.
history.lesson: A Hormuz closure is the tail risk India's oil-security planning exists for, and it has now happened.

today:
As of [[val:date]], Brent is at [[val:brent]] a barrel, up [[val:brent_3m]] over three months. The Hormuz route remains closed and attacks on Gulf shipping continue despite emergency stock releases. The rupee is at [[val:usdinr]] per dollar, and consumer inflation has climbed to [[val:cpi]], up [[val:cpi_3m]] in three months as fuel and transport costs feed through.

This is a textbook supply-led shock, and its end will come from the route, not from demand. Watch for any credible deal to reopen the strait, the pace of emergency stock releases, freight and insurance rates for Gulf voyages, and whether the government asks fuel retailers to hold pump prices or cuts fuel taxes. The first sign of ships moving freely again is likely to matter more than any oil forecast.
sowhat:
Treat the current rise as supply-led: there is no cyclical upside in it for India.

  • Be careful with heavy users of oil and its derivatives: airlines, paints, tyres, chemicals and logistics. Their margins feel it a quarter or two later.
  • Watch policy risk in state-run fuel retailers, which may be asked to hold pump prices, and in upstream producers, whose windfall can be taxed away as in 2022.
  • Rate-sensitive and richly valued stocks suffer indirectly through the weaker rupee, higher inflation and a tighter RBI.
  • Relatively insulated are businesses with domestic revenue, low energy intensity and pricing power.

The single most important signpost is the Hormuz route reopening. When it does, the war premium can vanish quickly, and the stocks hurt most by oil, such as airlines, paints and fuel retailers, have historically been the first to bounce.
